content.text:
Normal force: N = mg − T sinθ. Acceleration: a = [T cosθ − μ(mg − T sinθ)]/m.

Numbers (g = 9.8): cos20 = 0.9397, so T cosθ = 56.38 N. sin20 = 0.3420, so T sinθ = 20.52 N. N = 98 − 20.52 = 77.48 N. Friction = 0.25 × 77.48 = 19.37 N. Net force = 37.01 N, so a = 3.70 m/s². With g = 10: N = 79.48 N, friction = 19.87 N, net = 36.51 N, so a ≈ 3.65 m/s².

D: At 30°, T sinθ = 30 N, so N = 68 N and friction = 17 N. Friction decreases. The crate stays on the floor because 30 N is less than mg.

answers.brief_reasoning: Four forces: gravity mg downward, normal force N upward, tension T at 20° above horizontal in the direction of motion, kinetic friction f horizontal opposite motion.
answers.final_answer: Arrows from dot: weight (mg, down), normal (N, up), tension (T, 20° above horizontal, forward), kinetic friction (f, horizontal, backward)

answers.brief_reasoning: Vertical: N + T sinθ = mg, so N = mg − T sinθ. Horizontal: T cosθ − μN = ma.
A larger angle gives a larger vertical component T sinθ, so N = mg − T sinθ gets smaller and f = μN gets smaller (19.4 N → 17 N).

There are four forces: weight mg pointing straight down, normal force N pointing straight up, tension T along the rope at 20° above the horizontal in the direction of motion, and kinetic friction f_k pointing horizontally opposite the motion.
answers.final_answer: Draw four arrows starting on the dot: weight (F_g = mg) down; normal force (F_N) up; tension (T) at 20° above the horizontal toward the direction of motion; kinetic friction (f_k) horizontal, opposite the motion.

answers.brief_reasoning: Vertical: the crate does not accelerate vertically, so N + T sinθ = mg, giving N = mg − T sinθ. Horizontal: T cosθ − μN = ma.

Using g = 9.8 m/s²: T cos20° = 46.98 N and T sin20° = 17.10 N. Then N = 98 − 17.10 = 80.9 N, friction = 0.3 × 80.9 = 24.27 N, net force = 46.98 − 24.27 = 22.71 N, so a = 22.71/10 ≈ 2.27 m/s². With g = 10 m/s² the result is about 2.2 m/s².

The angle rises to 35°. The upward part of the tension grows from 17.1 N to T sin35° ≈ 28.7 N, so N = mg − T sinθ drops to about 69.3 N. Since f_k = μN, the friction force falls from about 24.3 N to about 20.8 N.
answers.final_answer: It decreases: a larger angle means a larger upward tension component, which lowers the normal force, and f_k = μN.

answers.brief_reasoning: There are four forces. Gravity mg points straight down. The normal force N points straight up. Tension T points along the rope, 30° above horizontal in the direction of motion. Kinetic friction f points horizontally, opposite the motion.
answers.final_answer: Four arrows starting on the dot: weight (Fg = mg) pointing down, normal force (FN) pointing up, tension (T) at 30° above horizontal toward the direction of motion, and kinetic friction (fk) pointing horizontally backward.

answers.final_answer: a = [T cosθ − μ(mg − T sinθ)]/m = (T/m)(cosθ + μ sinθ) − μg

answers.brief_reasoning: N = 117.6 − 30 = 87.6 N, so friction f = 0.2 × 87.6 = 17.52 N. T cosθ = 51.96 N, so the net force is 34.44 N. Divide by 12 kg.
answers.final_answer: a ≈ 2.9 m/s² (2.87 m/s² using g = 9.8 m/s²; 2.83 m/s² using g = 10 m/s²)

answers.brief_reasoning: At 45°, the upward part of the tension, T sinθ, grows from 30 N to about 42.4 N. Since N = mg − T sinθ, the normal force gets smaller (still positive, about 75.2 N). Friction is f = μN, so friction gets smaller too, falling from about 17.5 N to about 15.0 N.
answers.final_answer: The friction force decreases. The upward part of the tension (T sinθ) gets bigger, so the normal force (N = mg − T sinθ) gets smaller, and friction (fk = μN) gets smaller with it.
